title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
description:
# Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array

A sorted array of unique integers can be rotated by moving a suffix to the front. For example, `[0,1,2,4,5,6,7]` may become `[4,5,6,7,0,1,2]`.

Given the rotated sorted array `nums`, return the minimum element in the array.

The array may also look unrotated, because rotating an array of length `n` exactly `n` times returns it to its original order. You must solve the problem in `O(log n)` time.

## Example 1

**Input:** nums = [3,4,5,1,2]

**Output:** 1

**Explanation:** The original sorted array was `[1,2,3,4,5]`.

## Example 2

**Input:** nums = [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]

**Output:** 0

## Example 3

**Input:** nums = [11,13,15,17]

**Output:** 11

**Explanation:** The array is already in sorted order.

## Constraints

* `n == nums.length`
* `1 <= n <= 5000`
* `-5000 <= nums[i] <= 5000`
* All values in `nums` are unique.
* `nums` is an ascending sorted array rotated between `1` and `n` times.

solutions.name: Binary Search Comparing Right End
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep a search window `[left, right]` that always contains the minimum. Compare `nums[mid]` with `nums[right]`. If `nums[mid]` is larger, the rotation drop must be to the right of `mid`; otherwise `mid` can still be the minimum, so keep the left side including `mid`.

## Key Insight

The right endpoint tells which sorted segment `mid` belongs to. This avoids neighbor checks and naturally handles the fully unrotated case because the minimum remains inside the window until `left == right`.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Explicit Rotation Point Search
solutions.description:
## Approach

First handle the already sorted case. Otherwise, binary search for the exact adjacent pair where the order drops: either `nums[mid] > nums[mid + 1]` or `nums[mid - 1] > nums[mid]`. Use `nums[0]` to decide whether `mid` is still in the left sorted segment or has crossed into the rotated tail.

## Key Insight

The minimum is the first value after the only descending edge. This route is useful pedagogically because it makes the rotation point explicit, but it also shows why unrotated arrays need a separate guard.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Lower Bound on Rotated Tail
solutions.description:
## Approach

After ruling out the unrotated case, the minimum is the first value smaller than `nums[0]`. Binary search the suffix positions `1..n-1` for the first index satisfying that predicate.

## Key Insight

This reframes the problem as a lower-bound search over a boolean condition: values in the original left segment are not smaller than `nums[0]`, while values in the rotated tail are smaller. It avoids adjacent-index checks entirely.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Recursive Right-End Binary Search
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the same right-end comparison recursively. A sorted subarray returns its left endpoint immediately. Otherwise, compare `nums[mid]` with `nums[right]` and recurse only into the half that still contains the rotation drop.

## Key Insight

The recursive form exposes the divide-and-conquer invariant: every call receives an interval containing the minimum. The sorted-interval shortcut also explains why a fully unrotated array is not a special failure case.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(log n)
